name: Tashkent International Airport
before:
Uzbekistan's main airport and second busiest in Central Asia after Almaty, only 12 km from the centre of Tashkent. It is the hub for Uzbekistan Airways.

There are two runways, both built to take large aircraft including the 787 and the A380, the longer at 4,000 metres. Since 2024 there has been a 24 room hotel for passengers inside the airport.

One thing to warn a driver about. Cars may pull up on the first floor for drop-offs but only for ten minutes. Cameras linked to the traffic control system issue an automatic fine after that, so a long goodbye is expensive.

The bigger news is that this airport has a closing date. A new Tashkent International Airport is being built in the Tashkent Region near Yangiyo'l, due to open in late 2030, and the existing airport is set to close once it does.

It is named after Islam Karimov, the first president of independent Uzbekistan.
after:
Uzbekistan's main airport and one of the busiest in Central Asia, handling almost 10 million passengers in 2025. It is about 6 km from the centre of Tashkent and is the hub for Uzbekistan Airways.

There are two runways, and the longer, at 4,000 metres, can take the A380. A 24 room hotel for transit passengers opened in the departure terminal in January 2024.

The bigger news is that work has started on a new Tashkent International Airport in the Tashkent Region, near Yangiyul. It is due to open in late 2030, and the existing airport is expected to close once it does.

The airport is named after Islam Karimov, the first president of independent Uzbekistan.

claims.claim: one of the busiest in Central Asia
claims.inAfter: one of the busiest in Central Asia
claims.note: Was 'second busiest in Central Asia after Almaty'. Only Wikipedia states the ranking outright. It held in 2025 but narrowly: Almaty 11.93 million (Astana Times, file astanatimes-almaty-2026), Tashkent almost 10 million, Astana 9.2 million (Qazinform, file qazinform-astana-2025), so it could flip within a year. Softened to what the WFP Logistics Cluster also says.

claims.claim: almost 10 million passengers in 2025
claims.note: Replaces the unconfirmed Central Asia ranking with the operator's figure, which is what tells an agent how busy it is. Wikipedia's article text still gives 8.7 million for 2024; its infobox gives 9,986,445 for 2025 against the operator's 9,964,602 as reported. Both round to almost 10 million.

claims.claim: about 6 km from the centre
claims.inAfter: It is about 6 km from the centre of Tashkent
claims.note: Was 'only 12 km'. The coordinates put the airport 5.5 km in a straight line from the GeoNames centre, so 12 km is 2.2 times the straight line, outside the sweep's tolerance. The WFP assessment says about 6 km. Travel pages range from 4 to 14 km, and the ones that say 12 km follow Wikipedia. No direction is given: from the GeoNames point the airport is east, from Amir Timur Square it is south, so a compass point would mislead one way or the other.

claims.claim: ten-minute drop-off on the first floor
claims.wasBefore: Cars may pull up on the first floor for drop-offs but only for ten minutes
claims.why: Confirmed only for August 2024 (UzDaily, 31 Aug 2024, and Wikipedia). The forecourt has been rebuilt since: in September 2025 Uzbekistan Airports described new arrival lanes with ten minutes free and more changes when the halls merge (Gazeta, 17 Sep 2025, just outside the 12-month window). Nothing from the last 12 months confirms the rule as it stands.

claims.claim: automatic camera fines
claims.wasBefore: Cameras linked to the traffic control system issue an automatic fine after that, so a long goodbye is expensive
claims.why: Same age problem, and Gazeta (Sep 2025) calls the departures system 'similar but not fully automated', which contradicts 'automatic'.

claims.claim: the airport has a closing date
claims.wasBefore: this airport has a closing date
claims.why: No closing date has been set. It is expected to close once the new airport opens.
